content: The World Health Organization (WHO) announced the publication of biographies for all members of the 2013–2014 WHO Guideline Development Group on nutrition actions. This announcement also included the scope and purpose of the guideline development meeting, which outlined the background and objectives for the participants being considered. The management of any declared conflicts of interest, whether perceived or actual, relevant to the guideline was summarized. When WHO relies on independent expert advice to make decisions or provide recommendations to member states or stakeholders, a conflict-of-interest analysis is mandatory. A conflict of interest refers to any declared interest by an expert that could influence or be perceived to influence their objectivity and independence in advising WHO. WHO’s conflict-of-interest rules aim to prevent situations that could compromise the work of the expert, the committee, or WHO as a whole. The inquiry into conflicts of interest extends to any interest that could reasonably be perceived to affect the expert’s role. Dr. Hector Bourges Rodriguez, chair of the Board of Directors of the Dannon Institute in Mexico (a non-profit organization promoting nutrition research), declared receiving funds as a chair honorarium from the institute, which is funded by Dannon Mexico, a subsidiary of The Dannon Company, Inc. Since Dannon does not produce products or make claims related to maize flour and cornmeal fortification, Dr. Bourges Rodriguez was allowed to fully participate in the deliberations and decision-making for this guideline. Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil, employed by the Micronutrient Initiative, an international non-governmental organization supporting food fortification programs, co-authored several systematic reviews and articles on food fortification. While she participated in the evidence deliberations for maize flour and cornmeal fortification, she recused herself from voting on the guideline. Dr. Lynette Neufeld, employed by the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, which supports food fortification programs and has conducted research in this area, also participated in the evidence deliberations but recused herself from voting on the guideline. Ms. Carol Tom, employed by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) on a project related to child blindness and micronutrients, and as a consultant for the East, Central, and Southern African Health Community (ECSA-HC) on food fortification, was deemed to have no conflict of interest. USAID is a U.S. government agency, and ECSA-HC is a regional association of health ministries. She was allowed to fully participate in the deliberations and decision-making. Other external experts declared their interests but did not participate in the deliberations or decision-making process. The WHO Secretariat will continue monitoring research developments in maize flour and cornmeal fortification, particularly in areas with limited or low-quality evidence. If the guideline requires an update or if concerns arise about its validity, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the update following WHO’s formal guideline development procedures.
